The advanced single-crystal superalloy EPM 102 was used in this study, which was developed in the High Speed Research – Enabling Propulsion Materials Program.
EPM 102 contains high levels of refractory metals and is highly susceptible to the formation of secondary reaction zones (SRZ) beneath diffusion aluminide coatings.
The carburization treatment involved a 2-hour soak at 1093°C in a gas mixture of 3.5% H2, 0.35% CH4, and 96.15% Ar.
Grit blasting the superalloy surface to a roughness of 1000-1800 nm Ra was found to be optimal for effective carburization and formation of fine-scale tantalum carbides.
A stress relief heat treatment at 1121°C for 4 hours prior to grit blasting and carburization helped increase the carbide depth from 48 μm to 62 μm in machined test specimens.
Carbide depths of 50-80 μm were achieved in the slab samples, 62 μm in the machined tensile specimens, and 76-99 μm in the turbine blade sections using the optimized carburization process.
The researchers examined carburization at 982°C, 1066°C, and 1093°C, with durations of 2 and 4 hours, to optimize the carbide depth while minimizing gamma prime (γ') coarsening.
After carburization, the samples were coated with a platinum aluminide (PtAl) bondcoat and aged at 1093°C for 400 hours to promote SRZ formation, which was then examined.
The literature cited the rhenium (Re) content, aluminum diffusion from the coating, and surface stresses as key factors influencing SRZ formation in these superalloys.
The stress relief heat treatment was believed to reduce surface stresses by recrystallizing a thin layer on the superalloy surface, improving the effectiveness of the subsequent carburization.
Grit blasting with 200 μm alumina media produced the optimal surface roughness of 1600-1800 nm Ra for achieving the desired carbide depths.
Fine-scale tantalum carbides (TaC) were the predominant carbide phase that formed during the carburization process.
No enrichment of rhenium (Re) or tungsten (W) was observed in the carbides, suggesting that topologically close-packed (TCP) phases were not forming.
The carburization treatment was effective in mitigating the formation of SRZ beneath the PtAl bondcoat after the 400-hour aging exposure.
The researchers established a laboratory-scale carburization facility at NASA Glenn Research Center to study the process in more detail after the end of the Enabling Propulsion Materials program.
